d.title: When cardinality climbs, each compact encoding gives something up
d.caption: One-hot on a thousand categories is a thousand columns of mostly zeros, most with too few ones to learn anything from. Every alternative fits by discarding something, and the question is which loss the model can afford.

d.title: Why the naive target encoding is the label in disguise
d.caption: A category with one row encodes to that row's own target. The feature then *is* the label for that row, cross-validation reports an excellent score, and in production the column carries no information at all. The size of the leak is inversely proportional to the category's size, so it is worst exactly where high cardinality made you want the encoding.

d.title: Weight of evidence puts a category on the model's own scale
d.caption: WoE is the category's log-odds minus the overall log-odds. A logistic regression is linear in log-odds, so a feature already on that scale enters the model as a straight line — which is why a scorecard can print a number of points per attribute and have it be exact rather than approximate.

d.title: Why the bins must be monotonic
d.caption: A non-monotonic WoE says risk rises with income, then falls, then rises. That is usually noise in a thin bin, and it is never something a scorecard can print — so the bins are merged until the direction is consistent, trading a little fit for a statement the business can act on.

d.title: The transform family is one knob: the power of x
d.caption: Log is the limit as the power goes to zero; square root is power ½; Box-Cox fits the power from the data. They differ in what input they accept and how hard they compress the tail — which is the whole basis for choosing between them.

d.title: Retransformation bias: exp of the mean is not the mean
d.caption: Model a log target, predict, exponentiate, and the answer is systematically **too low** — not sometimes, always. The prediction on the log scale is the mean of the logs, which back-transforms to roughly the median rather than the mean. On a revenue forecast that is a persistent shortfall nobody can explain.

items.desc: back-transforms to around the median

items.label: E[y] is larger, always
items.desc: by Jensen's inequality, for any spread

items.desc: a smearing estimate, or a GLM with a log link

d.title: Three ways to cut, and what each one assumes
d.caption: The method chooses what the bins are *for*. Equal-width gives edges a person can read and, on skewed data, bins that are empty or hold almost everything. Equal-frequency guarantees population and produces edges at arbitrary-looking values. Supervised bins use the target, so they must be fitted on training data only.

d.title: A duration usually beats any calendar component
d.caption: Days since signup, hours since last purchase, days until the contract ends — each is continuous, each carries recency, and each must be computed against a reference that **was known at the row's own time**. Measuring 'days since last purchase' against the dataset's maximum date is a leak: that date is in the future for every row but one.

d.title: A vocabulary, and no vocabulary at all
d.caption: Hashing maps each token to a column by hashing it: nothing to fit, nothing to store, and nothing that can leak. The cost is collisions — two words sharing a column — and the loss of any way to name a column afterwards, which rules it out whenever the model has to be explained.

d.title: The selection leak
d.caption: Choosing features by their correlation with the target, over the whole dataset, before splitting, is leakage — and a particularly convincing kind, because the selected features really do predict well on this data. d.title: What PCA computes, and what each piece is called
d.caption: Explained variance measures **spread, not usefulness**: a component can carry most of the variance and none of the signal, because nothing in the computation ever looked at the target. That is the single most important property of PCA to hold on to.
cells: the scores are the new features
the sum of the discarded eigenvalues

d.title: Scaling decides the answer PCA gives
d.caption: PCA maximises variance, and variance has units. Leave income in pounds beside age in years and the first component is almost entirely income — not because it matters more, but because its numbers are larger. Standardising first is what makes the question 'which directions co-vary' rather than 'which column has the biggest units'.
cells: binary variance depends on the rate

d.title: What separates a proxy from a leak is availability, not strength
d.caption: A feature that predicts the label almost perfectly is suspicious but not thereby a leak. The question is whether it will be **populated, in that form, at prediction time** — support tickets correlate with dissatisfaction because they share a cause, and that correlation is the point.

d.title: The checks, and which kind of leak each one catches
d.caption: No single check finds all three kinds, which is why the list is a list. The first is the cheapest and finds the most: a single feature with a suspiciously high score, on its own, is almost always a leak rather than a discovery.

d.title: What each split actually claims
d.caption: A split is a claim about the population the estimate generalises to. A random split claims performance on rows like these; a group split claims performance on entities never seen; a time split claims performance on a later period — which is the only period a deployed model ever sees.
cells: many rows per customer or device

d.title: Group splits: who, not what
d.caption: With many rows per entity, a random split puts the same customer on both sides, and the model scores well by recognising the customer rather than the pattern. The fix is to split the **entities** and then take their rows.

d.title: Each mistake has a signature you can read without running anything
d.caption: The point of a signature is that the review is cheap: a line, a pattern or an omission that is visible in the diff, with a one-line check that confirms or clears it. Reading in a fixed order matters because the earliest mistake invalidates everything measured after it.
